primary_sources: British Parliamentary Recruiting Committee, "Remember the Lusitania" poster, 1915

stimulus.source_note: British Parliamentary Recruiting Committee poster, 1915 (public domain; Library of Congress cph.3g10930). Text quoted from the poster itself.
stimulus.text: British recruiting poster, 1915. Large red letters at the top read "REMEMBER THE 'LUSITANIA'". Below, smaller print quotes a jury's verdict: the dead "died from their prolonged immersion and exhaustion in the sea eight miles south-south-west of the Old Head of Kinsale on Friday, May 7th, 1915, owing to the sinking of the R.M.S. 'Lusitania' by a torpedo fired without warning from a German submarine." The verdict calls the sinking a crime "contrary to international law" and charges "the officers of the said submarine and the Emperor and Government of Germany" with "wilful and wholesale murder." Large red letters at the bottom read "IT IS YOUR DUTY TO TAKE UP THE SWORD OF JUSTICE TO AVENGE THIS DEVIL'S WORK" and "ENLIST TO-DAY". Small print at the bottom names the Parliamentary Recruiting Committee, London.

source: original; stimulus quoted from the British Parliamentary Recruiting Committee poster, 1915
stem: The poster's main purpose was to

options.text: warn British civilians to stay away from the sea
options.misconception: The poster says nothing about avoiding the sea. Its last words are a call to enlist.

options.text: demand that the United States declare war on Germany
options.misconception: The poster is British, published in London in 1915, two years before the United States entered the war. It speaks to British men, not to the United States.

options.text: persuade British men to enlist by calling the sinking murder
announce that Germany had apologized for sinking the Lusitania
options.misconception: The poster charges Germany with murder; it does not report an apology. Germany never apologized for the sinking.

rationales.A: The poster says nothing about avoiding the sea. Its last words are a call to enlist.
rationales.B: The poster is British, published in London in 1915, two years before the United States entered the war. It speaks to British men, not to the United States.
rationales.C: The poster calls the sinking wilful and wholesale murder, then says it is the reader's duty to take up the sword of justice and enlist. The charge of murder is the reason to join.
rationales.D: The poster charges Germany with murder; it does not report an apology. Germany never apologized for the sinking.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the poster's last words. It tells the reader to enlist today.
2. Work back to the reason it gives. It quotes a verdict calling the sinking murder, contrary to international law.
3. Notice who made it. Background from the books: the Parliamentary Recruiting Committee made posters to fill British ranks, and the sinking gave it a vivid reason to enlist.
Remember: a recruiting poster argues by giving you a reason to join, so find the reason before you name the purpose.
